summary:
Few Earth analog sites exist today for astronaut training and instrument testing ahead of Artemis and Mars missions, and most were picked by convention rather than global data. MoonSiteUA finds places on Earth that closely match future Moon bases and Mars landing sites, explains where each candidate fits and where it falls short, and lets citizen explorers check them in the field.

Our engine, Analog Finder, compares 7.9 million land cells (0.05° grid) against 1,345 lunar and Martian sites using NASA datasets: LRO LOLA, MGS MOLA, MODIS, GPM IMERG, ASTER GED, and MERRA-2. It scores three mission profiles (Artemis south-pole base, caves and lava tubes, and Mars astrobiology), links each candidate to a specific "planetary twin," and checks OpenAlex literature counts so unexplored sites stand apart from well-studied ones.

The scoring recovers the benchmark analogs agencies already use: Atacama ranks in the 100th percentile for Mars, the McMurdo Dry Valleys reach the 99.99th for the Moon, and 78% of confirmed lava tubes fall in the top 5% of the map. On the web app, explorers upload photos and measurements, validate sites through consensus beacons, and build shared virtual bases.
details:
Built for the "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars" challenge, MoonSiteUA combines satellite discovery, field verification, and community-built virtual bases.

What it does and how it works

To compare terrain directly across planets, we compute slopes, local relief, and roughness at two scales using the same pipeline on Earth (Copernicus GLO-90), the Moon (LRO LOLA), and Mars (MGS MOLA), all at roughly 400 m per pixel. Each Earth cell is matched to its "planetary twin," the closest lunar or Martian block. We also include environmental layers from MODIS, GPM IMERG, ASTER GED, MERRA-2, GLiM, and the Smithsonian GVP covering cold and frozen ground, bare soil, low sun, ice-free land, volcanism, rock type, basaltic rock, aridity, thermal range, albedo, and dust.

Mission scores use Index = Σ wᵢ·dᵢ / Σ wᵢ, where each dimension is scaled between 0 and 1 and weighted explicitly for three profiles: an Artemis south-pole base, caves and lava tubes (against LROC pits and Mars cave candidates), and Mars astrobiology (rover landing sites). To make sure results aren't sensitive to a single choice of weights, we resample the weights at random 200 times and keep only candidate zones that stay in the top 1% in at least half of the draws. We then exclude 32 known analogs and query OpenAlex for how many papers already cite each candidate as an analog; multiplying Discovery = Index × Novelty lets unstudied locations rise in the ranking.

In validation, Atacama lands in the 100th percentile for Mars and the McMurdo Dry Valleys in the 99.99th for the Moon. An independent check against OpenStreetMap puts 78% of confirmed lava tubes (94 entrances across 34 zones) in the top 5% of the map.

The web app

  • Explore: Interactive maps covering 56 real sites, with rankings, radar charts comparing each spot against known analogs, planetary twin links, adjustable profile weights, and a "Contribute data" panel.
  • Game: Three modes built on the real dataset: analog duel, find the twin, and "studied or undiscovered?".
  • Field verification: Explorers can upload photos along with temperature, humidity, and air quality measurements, or propose new points (at least 6 km apart, capped at 5 per explorer per day). Consensus beacons shift from grey (discovery) to orange (2–3 independent explorers) and green (5–10 explorers).
  • Community: Validated zones turn into virtual bases that grow floor by floor as people join and furnish rooms. Moon Coins unlock virtual items, rare Mars Coins go toward physical rewards, and missions steer contributors toward data gaps.

Dedicated Method, Validation, Safety, and Data pages document every formula, source, and limitation. The site is bilingual (Spanish/English) and includes a 30-second pitch video.

Benefits and intended impact

Space agencies and universities get a reproducible shortlist of analog sites for astronaut training and instrument testing, along with why each match works and what Earth cannot imitate (gravity, radiation, vacuum). Including literature novelty highlights high-scoring candidates that researchers haven't looked at yet.

Citizen science adds ground-level observations that satellites cannot measure and builds a community around Artemis and Mars exploration. Sites that are dangerous or hard to reach, like deep caves and volcanic vents, remain closed to the public and are routed to drone or rover missions with partner institutions (Tier 3).

Tools and technologies

  • Data processing: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, rasterio, h5py, netCDF4, pyhdf, shapely, H3) and NASA's earthaccess library for Earthdata downloads, plus Google Earth Engine (JavaScript).
  • Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn on Python, SQLite, scrypt password hashing, and pytest (60 tests).
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using three.js r128 for 3D coins, dioramas, and the beacon simulator, alongside d3-geo, topojson-client, and world-atlas for the maps.
  • Build: A Node.js script generates the 11 pages in both languages from one template. Code is hosted on GitHub, with a static copy served on GitHub Pages.

What makes it creative

Instead of relying on climate alone, we run the same terrain metrics across Earth, the Moon, and Mars and pair every Earth location with a concrete planetary twin. Scoring how unexplored a place is alongside its similarity keeps overlooked candidates from getting buried behind famous analogs, while field check-ins and base building turn the catalog into something people can verify and expand.

Factors we considered

Each site lists where it fails to match its planetary target, and we document the limits of our validation, including OpenStreetMap's bias toward visited places and GPM rainfall artefacts near coasts. In the database itself, NASA-derived points are locked so they cannot be edited or deleted.

Accounts are restricted to one per person via unique phone numbers, usernames, and emails, and an offline expedition mode runs a geofence check on sync so uploads made far from a site are blocked. We follow GDPR, do not collect national ID numbers, and route hazardous sites to robotic missions rather than public visits. Rewards use original designs with no NASA logos (since NASA insignia require permission for merchandise), and all underlying data are public and open.
